title: l2/l2 Sparse Recovery via Weighted Hypergraph Peeling
authors: Nick Fischer (Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Germany), Vasileios Nakos (National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and Archimedes / Athena RC, Greece)
abstract: We demonstrate that the best k-sparse approximation of a length-$n$ vector can be recovered within a $(1+\epsilon)$-factor approximation in $O( (k/\epsilon) \log n)$ time using a non-adaptive linear sketch with $O((k/\epsilon) \log n)$ rows and $O(\log n)$ column sparsity. This improves the running of the fastest-known sketch [Nakos, Song; STOC '19] by a factor of $\log n$, and is optimal for a wide range of parameters. Our algorithm is simple and likely to be practical, with the analysis built on a new technique we call weighted hypergraph peeling. Our method naturally extends known hypergraph peeling processes (as in the analysis of Invertible Bloom Filters) to a setting where edges and nodes have (possibly correlated) weights.

Abstract—We demonstrate that the best k-sparse approximation of a length-n vector can be recovered within a (1+ϵ)-factor
approximation in O((k/ϵ) log n) time using a non-adaptive
linear sketch with O((k/ϵ) log n) rows and O(log n) column
sparsity. This improves the running of the fastest-known sketch
[Nakos, Song; STOC ’19] by a factor of log n, and is optimal
for a wide range of parameters.
Our algorithm is simple and likely to be practical, with the
analysis built on a new technique we call weighted hypergraph
peeling. Our method naturally extends known hypergraph peeling
processes (as in the analysis of Invertible Bloom Filters) to a
setting where edges and nodes have (possibly correlated) weights.

I. I NTRODUCTION
The sparse recovery problem poses a deceptively simple yet
profound question: Is it possible to approximately reconstruct
the best k-term approximation of a vector x ∈ Rn using
only a few linear queries, and how efficiently can this be
achieved? This question, in its various forms and under different constraints on the queries and computational resources, is
a central challenge in fields like signal processing [1]–[3], data
compression [33], streaming algorithms under the name of the
heavy hitters problem [4], [32], as well as applied mathematics, usually in the form of combinatorial group testing [9]. By
focusing on the recovery of sparse vectors—where most of
the energy is concentrated in a small number of coordinates—
research in this area has unlocked new possibilities across a
wide range of applications, from MRI imaging [28], [36] to
real-time data analysis [33]. The exploration of this problem
has fundamentally transformed how we handle vast amounts
of data, enabling more efficient data storage, transmission, and
processing in diverse industries [10], [23], [28], [36].
In this paper, we focus on one of the most well-studied
forms of the sparse recovery problem [4], [7], [15], [16], [40],
[42], [43]. The goal is to design a (typically randomized)
matrix A ∈ Rm×n that satisfies the following criteria: (i) given
the measurement Ax for x ∈ Rn , we can recover a vector x′
that retains most of the energy from the top k coordinates of x,
(ii) the number of rows (also referred to as measurements),
m, is minimized, (iii) the encoding time, corresponding to the

only be achieved through the use of randomness [6], i.e.,
no deterministic matrix can recover all vectors. Specifically,

our approach is distinct and provides deeper insights into the

II. T ECHNICAL OVERVIEW
In this section we give a high-level overview of our new
sketch. It relies on hashing at its main building component,
similarly to [16], [40] and in all the heavy hitters literature.
However, our specific approach differs quite substantially from
previous work. We briefly review the two known approaches.
Known Approaches—Iterative and Hierarchical: In [16]
the vector x is hashed to O(k/ϵ) buckets, augmented with an
appropriate error-correcting code in such a way that from all
buckets that contain only one heavy hitter that heavy hitter

say k/2, of the heavy hitters to be isolated in their respective
buckets. So letting x′ denote the resulting recovered vector,
there are still up to k/2 heavy hitters remaining in the residual
vector x−x′ . To recover these, one can proceed in an iterative
fashion, i.e., we essentially repeat the same hashing process
where the number of buckets can be reduced by a constant
factor. This process can be set up in a such way that eventually,
after O(log k) rounds, it yields a vector satisfying the ℓ2 /ℓ2
guarantee. Due to the iterative procedure, one has to pay at
least one log n factor in the column sparsity and decoding
time. For details, we refer to [16].
In contrast, the improved algorithm in [40] builds a
log(k/ϵ)/ log log(k/ϵ)-degree interval tree over [n] and traverses that tree from top to bottom in order to find where
the heavy hitters are, recognizing heavy intervals per level. At
each level elements belonging to the same interval are hashed
to the same bucket and combined with gaussians, instead of
the usual random signs. The choice of gaussians is crucial in
order to reduce the likelihood of cancellation, and using the
anti-concentration of the gaussian distribution it is shown that
most energy from heavy hitters is retained if one sets up that
process correctly. The branching factor of this process yields
one additional log factor in the decoding time, and changing
the branching factor crucially affects correctness. For more
details, we refer to [40].
New Approach—One-Shot: In a nutshell, as we are
aiming for the best-possible O((k/ϵ) log n) recovery time,
our goal is to perform one-shot recovery rather than iterative
recovery (as in [16]) or hierarchical recovery (as in [40]). That
is, we will throughout consider a single hashing scheme.
Before we get into the details of our new approach, let us
first fix some definitions. We call i a heavy hitter (or just
heavy) if |xi |2 ≥ kϵ · ∥x−k ∥2 , and otherwise we call i light.
Let T ⊆ [n] denote the set of the largest k entries in x.
Following [40], instead of computing x′ directly we resort to a
slight simplification of the original task: It suffices to recover
a subset of heavy hitters R with the property that we do not

One can then easily refine R to derive the desired approximation x′ of x. For the rest of this overview we elaborate on

And as the number of vertices (i.e., buckets) is larger than

the hypergraph is quite sparse. In such a situation one can
prove that with constant probability all connected components
are loosely connected and therefore peelable, at least as long
as h ≥ 2 (for h ≥ 3 this event even happens with high
probability).
This peeling process technique has already been used before
in sparse recovery [11], [34], [42]. In [42] the support of the
vector x is known and thus the algorithm is concerned solely
about estimation rather than the harder task of identification,
whereas in [11], [34] the authors assume that the vector is
exactly k-sparse. In our case, where we assume nor knowledge
of the support nor exact sparsity, analyzing this process is quite
different and more challenging.

Problem 1: Not All Edges Are Peelable: The first serious
problem is that, in contrast to the unweighted setting, it is
unfortunately not true that all edges are peelable with high
probability.4 Does this mean that our approach is doomed?
Recall that it is not strictly necessary to recover all heavy
hitters, but that we can afford to miss a small fraction (energywise). Therefore, the question is whether we can recover edges
of sufficiently large total energy.
Our analysis of this step turned out to be surprisingly
clean. In fact, we only care about two aspects of G: (1) The

are chosen randomly with expected weight µ (though they

that any edge e fails to be peelable with probability at most
O(µ/we ).

A. Hypergraph Peeling
An h-uniform hypergraph G= (V, E) consists of vertices
V and hyperedges E ⊆ Vh (i.e., each hyperedge is a
size-h set of vertices). A 2-uniform hypergraph is simply a
graph, and many of the basic concepts on graphs generalize
to h ≥ 3. For u, v ∈ V , a u-v-path is a sequence of
vertices u = u1 , . . . , uℓ = v such that each pair {ui , ui+1 }
appears in a some hyperedge. We call u, v connected if there
exists a u-v-path, and we define their distance d(u, v) as the
length of the shortest u-v-path. For sets S, T ⊆ V , we set
d(S, T ) = mins∈S,t∈T d(s, t). The hypergraph G is connected
if all pairs of nodes are connected, and we call a maximal connected subhypergraph a connected component. We typically
denote by C(v) and C(e) the connected component containing
a vertex v ∈ V or a hyperedge e ∈ E.
A connected h-uniform hypergraph G = (V, E) is a
hypertree if |V | = (h − 1)|E| + 1. It is easy to verify that
this is the largest number of nodes in a connected hypergraph
with |E| hyperedges. If instead |V | = (h − 1)|E| we call G
unicyclic. See Section III-A for an illustration.

Lemma 27 (Running Time). The recovery algorithm runs in
time O((k/ϵ) log n) with high probability.
Proof. The first step is to bound the number of iterations of
the while-loop in Lines 2 to 9 by O(|V | + |R|). Let us call an
iteration successful if the condition in Line 8 is not fulfilled.
Observe that in each successful iteration we increase |Q| by 2
and increase |R| by 1, whereas in each unsuccessful iteration
we decrease |Q| by 1 and leave R unchanged. Thus, there can
clearly be at most |R| successful iterations, and consequently
at most |V | + 2|R| unsuccessful iterations.
Next, we bound the running time of a single iteration. The
time to pick v ∈ Q in Line 3 is negligible. Let us ignore
Line 4 for a moment. Computing the string y in Line 5
essentially amounts to computing the median of the values

also runs in time O(log n) by Lemma 9. Lines 8 and 9 are
again negligibly fast. Thus, disregarding the computation of
the values pv,j in Line 4, the time per iteration is O(log n).

for the three buckets v ∈ ei in time O(log n). It follows that
the total time is O((|V | + |R|) log n).
